meta.name: VMware Certified Professional - Data Center Virtualization (2V0-21.23)
meta.notes: [initial release: 12 questions covering core VCP-DCV / vSphere 8 domains — ESXi architecture, vCenter Server, vMotion, Storage vMotion, vSphere HA, DRS, vSAN, vSphere Distributed Switch, Fault Tolerance, vSphere Lifecycle Manager, resource controls, snapshots; balanced answer positions (3A/3B/3C/3D); operator-lens phrasing throughout]

questions.question: An administrator is asked to describe the hypervisor architecture of VMware ESXi to a new team member. Which statement BEST characterizes ESXi?
options: It is a bare-metal (Type 1) hypervisor whose VMkernel runs directly on server hardware
It is a hosted (Type 2) hypervisor that runs on top of a general-purpose operating system
It is a Linux distribution with KVM that VMware re-brands and supports commercially
It is a container runtime that schedules workloads on top of a host OS kernel
questions.explanation: ESXi is a Type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisor: the VMkernel boots directly on the server hardware and partitions CPU, memory, storage and networking among virtual machines without an underlying host OS. Type 2 hypervisors such as VMware Workstation run on top of an existing operating system. ESXi is not a Linux distribution — although it includes some open-source userworld components, its VMkernel is a proprietary microkernel. Container runtimes (containerd, CRI-O) share a host OS kernel and do not virtualize hardware the way ESXi does.

questions.question: A customer is deploying vCenter Server 8 from scratch and wants the VMware-supported, appliance-based form factor. Which option should they select?
options: A Windows Server VM with the vCenter Server for Windows installer
The vCenter Server Appliance (VCSA), a preconfigured Photon OS-based virtual appliance
A self-built Linux VM with the vpxd binaries copied from an ESXi host
A bare-metal install of vCenter directly on the management server
questions.explanation: Starting with vSphere 7, vCenter Server is delivered exclusively as the vCenter Server Appliance (VCSA) — a preconfigured Linux (Photon OS) virtual appliance that bundles vpxd, the embedded vPostgres database, the VAMI and the Single Sign-On services. vCenter Server for Windows was deprecated in 6.7 and removed in 7.0, so a Windows-based install is no longer supported. Hand-built Linux deployments or bare-metal installs are not supported configurations and would not pass VMware's lifecycle or upgrade checks.

questions.question: An administrator wants to live-migrate a running VM from ESXi host A to ESXi host B with no guest downtime, while both hosts continue accessing the VM's existing datastore. Which feature performs this operation?
options: Cold migration, which requires the VM to be powered off before moving it
Storage vMotion, which moves only the VM's files between datastores
vMotion, which transfers the VM's active memory and execution state between hosts over a vMotion-enabled VMkernel
vSphere Replication, which asynchronously copies a VM to a recovery site
questions.explanation: vMotion live-migrates a running VM's CPU and memory state between ESXi hosts that share access to the VM's storage, with sub-second switchover and no guest downtime; it requires a VMkernel adapter tagged for vMotion on each host and CPU compatibility (or EVC). Cold migration is offline. Storage vMotion changes the VM's underlying datastore, not its compute host. vSphere Replication is an asynchronous DR tool that produces point-in-time recovery copies — it does not provide live migration.

questions.question: A running production VM must be moved from an aging FC LUN to a newer all-flash datastore without taking the guest offline. Which vSphere capability is designed for exactly this task?
options: Cold storage migration via the datastore browser
Cross vCenter Server migration to a different SSO domain
vSphere Replication with planned failover to the new datastore
Storage vMotion, which live-migrates a powered-on VM's files to a different datastore
questions.explanation: Storage vMotion live-migrates the .vmx, VMDK and supporting files of a powered-on VM from one datastore to another with no guest downtime, optionally converting disk format (thin/thick) along the way. Cold storage migration requires powering the VM off. Cross vCenter migration moves the VM between vCenter inventories but is not the canonical answer for a simple intra-cluster datastore swap. vSphere Replication produces asynchronous DR copies rather than performing an in-place datastore relocation of the running VM.

questions.question: After an ESXi host suffers a hardware failure, the administrator notices that its VMs have automatically powered back on across the remaining cluster hosts. Which feature provided this behavior?
options: Distributed Resource Scheduler (DRS), which rebalances load across hosts
vSphere High Availability (HA), which restarts VMs from a failed host on the surviving hosts
Fault Tolerance (FT), which keeps a continuous mirrored secondary VM running
vSAN stretched cluster witness, which arbitrates split-brain conditions
questions.explanation: vSphere HA monitors hosts in the cluster and, when a host fails, restarts the VMs that were running on it on the remaining hosts after a short reboot window — this matches the described power-on behavior. DRS handles ongoing load balancing and initial placement but does not restart VMs after a host failure. FT keeps a lockstep secondary VM live with no power-off at all, so a 'power back on' event would not occur. The vSAN witness arbitrates storage object availability across sites and does not by itself restart VMs.

questions.question: A vSphere cluster has eight hosts of varying CPU and memory utilization. The administrator wants vCenter to automatically place new VMs on the least-loaded host and to vMotion running VMs between hosts to keep utilization even. Which feature should be enabled?
options: Distributed Resource Scheduler (DRS) in fully automated mode
vSphere High Availability admission control
Storage DRS (SDRS) on the shared datastore cluster
Enhanced vMotion Compatibility (EVC) at the cluster level
questions.explanation: DRS handles two related jobs: initial placement (choosing the best host for a powered-on VM) and ongoing load balancing via automatic vMotion when the cluster imbalance metric exceeds the configured threshold. Setting DRS to fully automated lets vCenter execute the recommendations without operator approval. HA admission control reserves capacity for failover but does not balance load. Storage DRS balances VMDK placement across datastores, not VMs across hosts. EVC only normalizes CPU feature sets so vMotion can succeed between mixed-generation CPUs — it does not itself move workloads.

questions.question: A team is designing shared storage for a vSphere cluster using only the local NVMe drives in each ESXi host, with no external SAN or NAS. Which VMware technology pools those local drives into a single distributed datastore?
options: VMFS-6, formatted on a Fibre Channel LUN presented by an external array
NFS 4.1, exported from a dedicated file-server VM running on one of the hosts
Raw Device Mapping (RDM), passing each physical disk through to a guest VM
vSAN, which aggregates host-local disks into a software-defined shared datastore
questions.explanation: vSAN is VMware's hyper-converged storage layer: it claims local SSD/NVMe and optional capacity-tier drives across cluster hosts and presents a single distributed datastore protected by storage policies. VMFS-6 is a clustered file system that sits on top of an external block LUN — it does not pool local disks across hosts. NFS 4.1 requires an external file server (or a single-host appliance that becomes a bottleneck) rather than a peer-to-peer pool. RDM exposes one LUN to one guest and is the opposite of aggregating storage.

questions.question: A datacenter has six ESXi hosts that should share a consistent set of port groups, VLANs and traffic-shaping policies managed centrally from vCenter. Which networking construct best fits this requirement?
options: A vSphere Standard Switch (vSS) configured identically on each host by the local administrator
Per-host Ethernet ifcfg files synchronized with a configuration-management tool
A vSphere Distributed Switch (vDS), which spans all hosts and is managed centrally by vCenter
A NIC team configured directly on each physical adapter, without any virtual switch
questions.explanation: A vSphere Distributed Switch is created and configured once in vCenter and then attached to multiple ESXi hosts — port groups, VLANs, uplinks, NIOC and traffic policies are managed at the vDS level so every member host stays in sync. Standard switches are per-host objects and drift between hosts unless something else keeps them aligned. ESXi does not use ifcfg files for vSwitch configuration. Configuring NIC teaming alone on physical adapters skips the virtual-switch layer entirely and cannot expose port groups, VLANs or vMotion-tagged VMkernels to VMs.

questions.question: A mission-critical VM must keep running with zero downtime — not even a brief HA restart — if its ESXi host fails. Which vSphere feature provides this guarantee?
options: Fault Tolerance (FT), which maintains a lockstep secondary VM on a second host
vSphere High Availability (HA) with Proactive HA enabled
Microsoft Failover Clustering inside the guest OS, layered on top of vSphere
vSphere Replication with a short Recovery Point Objective
questions.explanation: FT continuously mirrors the primary VM's CPU and memory state to a secondary VM on another host using Fast Checkpointing; if the primary fails, the secondary takes over instantly with no guest reboot and zero downtime — the only vSphere-native feature that meets a strict zero-downtime SLA. HA, even with Proactive HA, still incurs a VM restart on the surviving host after a failure event. Guest-level clustering (e.g. WSFC) needs application support and is application-specific. vSphere Replication is asynchronous DR and yields an RPO, not continuous availability.

questions.question: An administrator wants to patch every ESXi host in a cluster to a known-good image (ESXi base + vendor add-on + firmware) declaratively and let vCenter remediate hosts one at a time. Which tool should be used?
options: vSphere Update Manager (VUM) baselines, still the primary tool in vSphere 8
Manual esxcli software profile update commands run on each host over SSH
vSphere Lifecycle Manager (vLCM) image-based cluster remediation
VMware Tools Lifecycle Manager, which updates the guest OS tools package
questions.explanation: vSphere Lifecycle Manager introduced a desired-state image model (ESXi base + vendor add-on + firmware/HSM components) applied to a whole cluster; vLCM drift-detects each host and remediates them in maintenance-mode rolling order — the current best-practice for cluster patching from vSphere 7 onward, fully supported in vSphere 8. The legacy VUM baseline workflow has been subsumed by vLCM. Hand-running esxcli is unsupported at fleet scale. VMware Tools Lifecycle Manager only updates the guest VMware Tools package and does not touch ESXi or firmware.

questions.question: Within a DRS cluster, a tenant must be guaranteed at least 32 GHz of CPU and 64 GB of memory, while never consuming more than 64 GHz and 128 GB even when the cluster is idle. Which vSphere construct best expresses this requirement?
options: A VM-Host affinity rule pinning the tenant's VMs to specific hosts
A resource pool with reservations of 32 GHz / 64 GB and limits of 64 GHz / 128 GB
Per-VM CPU and memory shares set to High on each tenant VM
A storage policy that pins the VMs' VMDKs to flash-tier storage
questions.explanation: Resource pools are the canonical container for applying reservations (guaranteed minimum), limits (hard maximum) and shares (relative priority under contention) to a group of VMs — exactly the floor-and-ceiling SLA in the question. VM-Host affinity rules control where VMs run, not how much CPU/RAM they get. Shares only matter when the cluster is under contention and cannot guarantee an absolute floor or impose a ceiling. Storage policies govern VMDK placement and protection on vSAN/SPBM, not compute reservations.

questions.question: An administrator suggests using VMware snapshots as the primary long-term backup mechanism for production VMs. Why is this approach incorrect?
options: Snapshots can only be taken when the VM is powered off, so they cannot capture a running workload
Snapshots require the same vSphere license tier as Fault Tolerance and are usually disabled
Snapshots are stored on a separate vCenter database and disappear when vCenter is upgraded
Snapshots are short-lived, dependent on the parent VMDK chain, and grow delta files that degrade performance — they are not a backup and VMware recommends keeping them no longer than 24-72 hours
questions.explanation: VMware snapshots create delta (redo-log) files that capture changes since the snapshot was taken; they depend on the parent VMDK chain, expand continuously with guest writes, and degrade I/O performance the longer they live — VMware's KB guidance is to keep them short-lived (typically no more than 24-72 hours) and to use a backup product (which may briefly use a snapshot during its operation) for actual data protection. Snapshots are taken while a VM is running. They are a core platform feature, not gated by FT licensing. Snapshot metadata lives with the VM on its datastore, not in the vCenter database.
